withstand

/with-STAND/ - the stress falls on STAND · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Withstand means to endure or resist something successfully, without giving way.

Stadium glass must withstand a line drive off the bat without so much as a chip.

Example

Grandfather's mailbox has withstood forty years at the end of the lane: two blizzards a winter, one sideswipe from a snowplow, and the daily slam of a spring-loaded door. The post leans a little; the box itself has never let in a drop.

Withstand is the exact verb because it insists on success — to withstand something is to take its force and not give way. Endure only says you lasted through it, and survive allows for limping out broken; the mailbox comes through whole, which is the extra claim withstand makes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

endure: To endure is to last through something hard — the word measures time and says nothing about your condition at the end; you may come out whole or wrecked. Withstand adds the missing promise: you took the force and did not give way. Enduring is lasting; withstanding is lasting undamaged.

resist: To resist is to push back against a force — the emphasis is on the fight, and success is not guaranteed; you can resist fiercely and still lose. Withstand is scored on the outcome: whatever pushed, you did not give way. Resisting describes the effort; withstanding certifies the result.

weather: To weather something is to come through a storm or a rough patch, often scuffed and the worse for it. What withstand adds is the claim of coming through intact — no giving way, shape unchanged. A ship weathers the gale battered; a breakwater withstands it unmoved.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

buckle: to give way suddenly under the load

succumb: to stop resisting and be overcome

Where it sits · how unharmed you come through the blow

survive → withstand → shrug off

survive vs. withstand: Merely surviving is the lower bar — you come out alive but possibly broken — and it stops short of withstanding, which means taking the blow without giving way.

shrug off vs. withstand: Shrug off goes further than withstand — what you withstand tests you and leaves marks, while what you shrug off never seriously threatened you at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — with-: against, back (the prefix's old English sense)

Root — stand: to hold one's ground

Put it together: With- (against — the prefix's old meaning, not today's 'alongside') + stand = to stand against. Old English speakers who withstood an enemy literally stood their ground against him. The same fossil sense of with- hides in withhold (hold back) and withdraw (pull back); withstand is the one that kept its full fighting posture.

Use the root in a new word: standstill: The standstill on the bridge lasted until sunset.

Word Choice

neutral

Withstand is the verb of survival with your shape intact: it always takes an object — you withstand something — and it quietly promises success, no giving way. Endure emphasizes how long you lasted; resist, that you fought back. Pair it with this unit's robust: robust things are precisely the things that withstand.
